name: Machine Chest Press

claims.text: ACE sets the seat so the handles are level with the mid-chest (around nipple level) and no deeper than the front of the chest, with the back firmly against the backrest.

quotes.text: Sit with your back firmly supported against the backrest. Adjust the seat height so that the handles are level with your mid-chest (around nipple level) and the handles are positioned no deeper than chest level (level with the front of your chest).

claims.text: ACE asks for a full grip with the thumbs around the handles and a neutral wrist, in line with the forearm.

quotes.text: Grasp the handles firmly with a full grip (thumbs clasped around the handles) and maintain a neutral wrist position (i.e., wrists in line with your forearms).

claims.text: Feet go firmly on the floor or the foot rests; the abs are braced while the low back keeps its natural arch, neither pressed into the backrest nor arched further.

quotes.text: Position your feet firmly on the floor or on the foot rests to stabilize your body.
your abdominal muscles to stabilize your spine, but do not press your low back into the backrest. Maintain the natural arch in your low back and avoid arching your back throughout the exercise.

claims.text: The shoulders are pulled back and down before the press and held there for the whole exercise.

quotes.text: Depress and retract your scapulae (pull shoulders back and down) and attempt to hold this position throughout the exercise.

claims.text: The press extends the elbows forward, exhaling, with the wrist neutral and the head in line with the spine; so the elbows start bent. ACE gives no start elbow angle.

quotes.text: Gently exhale and slowly perform a pressing movement, extending your elbows infront, while maintaining a neutral wrist position, and keep your head aligned with your spine while avoiding any arching your low back.

claims.text: At full press the elbows are fully extended but not locked, and the shoulder blades are still in contact with the backrest, not rounding forward.

quotes.text: Continue pressing until your elbows are fully extended, but not locked. Your shoulder blades should continue to make contact with the backrest and not round or bend forward.

claims.text: After a momentary pause at full press, the elbows bend slowly and with control on the way back to the start. ACE gives no seconds.

quotes.text: Pause momentarily then gently allow your elbows to flex (bend) in a slow, controlled manner while returning the bar back towards the starting position.

claims.text: ACE says people very frequently press until the shoulder blades round forward off the backrest, that this makes the muscles holding the shoulder blades to the ribcage less stable, and that beginners should keep the blades flat on the backrest.

quotes.text: Very frequently individuals will press the bar to a point where the shoulder blades round themselves forward and move off the backrest. This promotes instability within the muscles that hold the shoulder blades to the ribcage.
focus initially on pressing while keeping your shoulder blades flat and firmly positioned against the backrest.

claims.text: In the lab study of this machine (20 physically active adults, 60% of 1RM), each lowering and each pressing phase took 2 seconds, paced by a metronome. This is a study protocol, not a coaching recommendation for beginners.

quotes.text: the eccentric phase and the concentric phase were performed and recorded at a velocity of two seconds in each phase
Twenty physically active adults performed a set of 8 repetitions at 60% of the one repetition maximum.

claims.text: On the seated chest press with a neutral grip, the upper (clavicular) chest worked at about 30% of maximum, more than on the flat bench press, and the front shoulder worked at about 24% in every exercise and grip tested.

quotes.text: the clavicular portion of the pectoralis major had significantly greater muscle activity in the seated chest press exercise with a neutral grip (~30% of the maximal voluntary isometric contraction (MVIC)) than in the lying bench press exercise with a prone grip at 150% of the biacromial width (~25% MVIC).
The muscle activity of the anterior deltoid was not significantly different across any exercise or grip evaluated (~24% MVIC).

claims.text: On the machine, the middle chest showed the highest activity, and the upper, middle and lower chest and the front shoulder did not differ significantly from each other, so the front shoulder works about as hard as the chest.

quotes.text: the PMMP showed the highest muscle activity in all exercises, except in the lying bench press exercise with a grip at 50% of the biacromial width.
There were no significant differences in the muscle activity between the upper, middle, and lower portions of the pectoralis major and the AD in any exercise evaluated

claims.text: The press works by extending the elbows, which is the triceps' action; inferred from the movement, not measured on this machine in the sources read.

quotes.text: perform a pressing movement, extending your elbows infront

claims.text: On the bench press (not the machine), keeping the handle low in the heel of the palm stacks it over the forearm bones; when the wrist bends back and the bar rolls into the fingers, it adds a lever at the wrist. Applied to machine handles by inference.

quotes.text: The bar should sit as low in the heel of the palm as possible – stacked directly over the forearm bones.
If the wrists bend back and the barbell rolls up into the fingers, that creates an unnecessary moment arm and an energy leak.

claims.text: In patients with pain on the back of the wrist when loading it bent back (push-ups, planks, yoga), MRI found a problem on the back of the wrist in 84%. It shows association in patients, not cause, and did not study pressing handles.

quotes.text: MRI demonstrated an identifiable dorsal abnormality in 84% of patients with dorsal wrist pain associated with weight bearing on the extended wrist.
Many exercise disciplines incorporate upper extremity weight-bearing exercises in an extended wrist posture, for example push-ups, plank position, and various yoga and Pilates poses.

claims.text: On the bench press at 50% of 1RM, an instruction to use only the chest raised chest activity by 22% without changing front-shoulder activity; the cue may work less well on heavy sets. Applied to the machine by inference.

quotes.text: During the 50% max lift with verbal instructions to focus on chest muscles, PM EMG activity increased by 22% over preinstruction activity (p = 0.005), whereas AD and TB activities were statistically unchanged.
verbal technique instruction is effective in shifting muscle activity during a basic lift, but it may be less effective at higher intensities.

sources.title: Comparison of Muscle Activity between the Horizontal Bench Press and the Seated Chest Press Exercises Using Several Grips (Muyor, Rodriguez-Ridao, Oliva-Lozano; J Hum Kinet 87:23-34)
Dorsal Wrist Pain in the Extended Wrist-Loading Position: An MRI Study (Nance et al., J Wrist Surg 6(4):276-279)
Effect of verbal instruction on muscle activity during the bench press exercise (Snyder, Fry; J Strength Cond Res 26(9):2394-400)

plate.equipment: Seated chest press machine (pivot arm or selectorized) with seat, back pad and handles; seat set so the handles meet the mid-chest (c1); feet on the floor or the foot rests (c3).
plate.start: Seated, back firmly against the backrest (c1); handles level with the mid-chest, around nipple level, and no deeper than the front of the chest, so the elbows are bent (c1, c5; no source gives a start elbow angle); full grip, wrists in line with the forearms (c2); shoulders back and down (c4); feet planted (c3).
plate.end: Elbows fully extended but not locked (c6); shoulder blades still in contact with the backrest, not rounded forward (c6); wrists neutral, head in line with the spine (c5).

checkpoints.label: Handles mid-chest
checkpoints.what: Set the seat so the handles start level with the middle of the chest.

checkpoints.label: Blades on pad
checkpoints.what: Shoulder blades stay in contact with the backrest through the whole press.

checkpoints.label: Not locked
checkpoints.what: Press until the elbows are straight, but not locked.

mistake.what: Shoulder blades round forward and come off the backrest at the end of the press.
mistake.why: ACE says individuals very frequently press to this point and that it makes the muscles holding the shoulder blades to the ribcage less stable. How often it happens is not measured.

tells.text: Shoulder blades stay on the pad
Elbows straight but not locked at the end

tempo.text: Lab pacing on this machine: 2 s pressing, 2 s lowering (study protocol, WEAK). ACE asks for a momentary pause at full press and gives no seconds, so pause is null.

grip.type: Full grip, thumbs around the handles (c2).
grip.width: Set by the machine handles; no source gives a width to choose.
grip.handContact: Handle low in the heel of the palm, stacked over the forearm bones (bench-press coach source applied to machine handles, MECH, c13).
grip.wrist: Neutral, in line with the forearm (c2, c5); not bent back with the handle in the fingers (c13).

setup.step: Set the seat so the handles are level with the middle of your chest, about nipple height.
Sit with your back firmly against the backrest.
Put your feet firmly on the floor or on the foot rests.
Take a full grip, thumbs around the handles, wrists in line with your forearms.
Pull your shoulders back and down, and hold them there.

posture.point: Brace your abs and keep the natural arch in your low back; do not press it into the pad or arch more.
Breathe out and press slowly, wrists straight, head in line with your spine.
Shoulder blades stay in contact with the backrest the whole time.
Press until your elbows are straight, but not locked.
Pause for a moment, then bend your elbows slowly, with control, back to the start.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Pressing until the shoulder blades round forward off the backrest.
handlingMistakes.fix: Keep your shoulder blades flat and firmly against the backrest as you press.

handlingMistakes.mistake: Wrist bent back, handle rolled up into the fingers.
handlingMistakes.fix: Set the handle low in the heel of your hand, with your wrist in line with your forearm.
Set the machine so the handles start no deeper than the front of your chest.

rows.means: Expected: on this machine the front of the shoulders works about as hard as the chest.
rows.fix: On lighter sets, think about pushing with your chest.

rows.means: Fault: the wrist bends back and the handle rolls into the fingers.
rows.fix: Set the handle low in the heel of your hand, wrist in line with your forearm.

rows.means: Fault: the elbows lock at the end of the press.
rows.fix: Stop the press with your elbows straight but not locked.

risks.risk: Shoulder blades coming off the pad makes the muscles that hold them to the ribcage less stable.
Wrist: pain on the back of the wrist when it is loaded bent back has been linked with problems found on scans there.

zooms.right: Full grip, thumb around the handle, handle low in the heel of the palm, wrist in line with the forearm.
zooms.wrong: Wrist bent back, handle rolled up into the fingers.

zooms.right: At full press, shoulder blades flat on the backrest, elbows straight but not locked.
zooms.wrong: Shoulder blades rounded forward, off the backrest.

zooms.right: Handles level with the middle of the chest, about nipple height.

add.why: The upper (clavicular) chest worked at about 30% of maximum on the machine with a neutral grip, more than on the flat bench (c10).

libraryDiff.why: chest primary stands: the middle chest showed the highest activity (c11). front_delts secondary stands: the front shoulder worked at about 24% and did not differ significantly from the chest (c10, c11). triceps secondary stands on the elbow-extending action (c12, MECH); no read source gives a triceps figure for this machine in text.

notes: Tempo: the only seconds for this exercise are the lab pacing in Muyor 2023 (c9, WEAK); no novice-level source giving seconds was found. Pause is null: ACE says "pause momentarily" with no seconds (c7).
Muyor 2023 describes thumbs "in a hook grip" on the machine; the card follows ACE's full grip with thumbs around the handles (c2).
Not sourced, so left out: a start elbow angle, a handle width to choose, an elbow-lockout injury mechanism, and a seat-too-low fault.

Golden-B sources weiss1995, fees1998, calatayud2016, nhs-wrist-pain and nhs-elbow-pain are not cited: Weiss is a splint/nerve-pressure study, the Fees abstract does not state a press-depth limit, Calatayud repeats Snyder's bench-press point, and the NHS pages belong to the shared red-flag boxes.
